en: Adding heat energy to ice causes its water molecules to vibrate faster and break their rigid bonds, turning the solid into liquid water.
When sunlight heats a puddle, the fastest-moving water molecules gain enough energy to escape the liquid surface and become invisible water vapor gas.
Cooling nighttime air slows down invisible water vapor molecules, causing them to clump together and form liquid dew drops on cold grass.
Stirring sugar into tea allows water molecules to surround and pull apart individual sugar crystals, spreading them evenly to create a sweet solution.
Exposing iron to oxygen and moisture triggers a chemical reaction that slowly transforms the shiny metal into a flaky, reddish-brown substance called rust.
Mixing baking soda and vinegar causes an acid-base chemical reaction that rapidly produces bubbles of carbon dioxide gas, making the mixture fizz.
Hot summer temperatures transfer heat to a metal bridge, making its atoms vibrate wider and cause the solid structure to physically expand.
Because oil molecules are less dense than water molecules, pouring oil into a glass of water causes it to float on top.
Placing liquid water in a freezer removes heat energy, slowing the molecules down until they lock into a rigid, hexagonal ice crystal structure.
Pouring a muddy mixture through filter paper separates the materials because the tiny paper holes trap solid sand while letting liquid water pass.
Leaving solid dry ice at room temperature causes its carbon dioxide molecules to absorb heat and skip the liquid phase, turning directly into gas.
Heating water increases the kinetic energy of its molecules, allowing them to break apart and dissolve more solid salt crystals than cold water can.
